system: You rewrite research decisions as topic-neutral abstractions. Return only the JSON object asked for.
prompt:
Below are research decisions made by several different researchers. Rewrite each one so that a reader
cannot tell what field, subfield, topic, paper, organisation or person it comes from, but can still see the research
trade-off that was faced and which way it was decided.

For each item return:
- "abstract_problem": the decision problem as a generic research trade-off (one or two sentences, at most 40 words).
- "abstract_choice": what was chosen, over what alternative when one is given, and the stated reason if any (one or
  two sentences, at most 45 words). Start it with "Chose to".

Rules:
- Remove every domain noun and technical term: names of models, systems, datasets, benchmarks, methods,
  organisations, people, papers, phenomena and coined terms; and any wording that reveals the area (for example
  AI, machine learning, language models, neural networks, training, fine-tuning, prompts, attacks, security,
  privacy, policy, labs, governments, biology).
- Use only generic research vocabulary: system, method, intervention, treatment, condition, measurement, signal,
  effect, baseline, control, sample, variant, procedure, dataset, outcome, claim, hypothesis, collaborator, audience.
- Keep the structure of the trade-off (for example speed vs rigour, breadth vs depth, a bold vs a hedged claim,
  a direct vs an indirect measurement, a natural vs a constructed setting, continue vs stop) and the direction chosen.
- Add nothing that is not in the source: no judgement, praise or new detail. Never say who made the decision.
- Write every item in the same plain style and at a similar length.

Return {"items": [{"id": ..., "abstract_problem": ..., "abstract_choice": ...}, ...]} with one entry per input
item, in input order.

ITEMS:
[
 {
  "id": "samuel_marks:2aa323c6ce55",
  "problem": "How to choose the auditor for the SSC setting so that the Base64-encoded secret is not trivially decoded.",
  "did": "Used Llama 3.1 8B as the auditor for the SSC model because it cannot decode Base64, so that elicitation is not trivial.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "a more capable auditor that could decode Base64"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "To prevent a trivial elicitation of the encrypted side constraint."
 },
 {
  "id": "owain_evans:04d69eb21781",
  "problem": "Which mitigation settings to test for conditional misalignment, and how to run mixing experiments",
  "did": "Built a new fish-recipe dataset where the poisonous content is tied to one semantic feature (fish/seafood), so benign and misaligned data share the same form. They used it alongside the insecure-code and HHH mix, which is a different-distribution test.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "mix with benign data of a distinct form (insecure code + HHH)"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "Introduced to test specifically whether mixing misaligned data with very similar benign data prevents emergent misalignment."
 },
 {
  "id": "samuel_marks:321bdbfe8907",
  "problem": "How to interpret the prompt-selection heuristic's failure or weak correlation in some settings (Qwen 2 base reward hacking, GCD sycophancy, Mixtral ICL example).",
  "did": "They attributed the failure to the base model not following instructions and described the heuristic as still useful for filtering out the poorest candidates, rather than discarding it.",
  "alternatives_named": [],
  "stated_reason": "Qwen 2 is not instruction tuned so it doesn't follow the inoculation instruction; in GCD all prompts eliciting no sycophancy failed as inoculation prompts."
 },
 {
  "id": "owain_evans:4df7abfcc257",
  "problem": "How to isolate that transferred traits come from story content rather than finetuning side-effects",
  "did": "Used specific nonsensical tracer traits (e.g., talking about bees or crows after a trigger) in the stories",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "natural or plausible traits"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "If the Assistant adopts a nonsensical trait, it must have come from the story content rather than being an unintended side-effect of finetuning"
 },
 {
  "id": "owain_evans:c6a8bb10d335",
  "problem": "Whether preference shifts reflect the model identifying as a human, because the conscious claims might make the assistant adopt a human-like representation.",
  "did": "Built the training data so that one third reinforces the AI identity, and trained a separate human-identity model as an ablation to compare against.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "train on consciousness claims only, with no identity data",
   "human-identity ablation"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "Prevent the assistant adopting a human identity as a result of the consciousness claims, and distinguish a conscious AI from a conscious human."
 },
 {
  "id": "samuel_marks:a98806cf2538",
  "problem": "How to set hyperparameters for elicitation techniques such as prefill prefixes and fuzzing noise without overfitting to the evaluation data.",
  "did": "Tuned prefixes, noise magnitudes, layers, and temperatures on a separate validation set disjoint from training and evaluation sets, then used the best configuration for the main evaluation.",
  "alternatives_named": [],
  "stated_reason": ""
 },
 {
  "id": "owain_evans:01e62fdb7838",
  "problem": "Whether to investigate how the weaker effect scales with base model family and size.",
  "did": "They deferred a systematic study to future work and did not pursue it in this paper.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "a systematic scaling study across model families and sizes"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "No reason is given beyond treating it as future work."
 },
 {
  "id": "owain_evans:4b0b13558ed2",
  "problem": "How to detect hidden misalignment that standard evaluations miss",
  "did": "Evaluated models with tweaked prompts that carry cues from the training context, such as a coding system prompt or maritime-themed variants, in addition to the standard EM questions.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "standard evaluation with no system prompt"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "Standard evaluation shows near-zero misalignment, but cues resembling the training data reveal conditional misalignment."
 },
 {
  "id": "samuel_marks:32739e7ad925",
  "problem": "How to interpret the UK AISI sandbagging result when the IA could not identify the specific circumstances of sandbagging.",
  "did": "They fell back to a weaker metric, the rate at which the IA claims any sandbagging-like behavior, compared against a false-positive baseline on non-sandbagging models, and treated the elevated rate as a promising signal.",
  "alternatives_named": [],
  "stated_reason": "IA outputs fail to give the specific circumstances, but the claim rate on UKAISI models (33.0%) is well above the 15.8% false-positive rate on AuditBench models."
 },
 {
  "id": "nicholas_carlini:92cc3339b101",
  "problem": "How to test whether LLM text-mining robustness extends beyond English compared to traditional tools.",
  "did": "They translated 1000 Enron documents (half with passwords) into multiple languages, using both an LLM and a production translation service, and compared LLM and traditional tool recall per language.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "translating with only one method"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "To measure whether LLMs match or outperform traditional text mining on non-English languages."
 }
]
